how-much-does-stockx-take-from-sellers.h.text:
← StockX seller payout calculator

How much does StockX take from sellers?

The headline "seller fee" is not one fixed percentage, and it is not the only deduction. What actually lands in your account after a sale depends on your Seller Level, whether you're enrolled in Fast Shipping, a flat payment processing percentage, and what you pay to ship the item to a verification center — and two sellers moving the identical item at the identical price can keep meaningfully different amounts.

Open the free payout calculator

What comes out of a sale before payout

Seller fee, scaled by your Seller Level. StockX's transaction fee percentage drops as your completed-sale count and account history improve. A newer seller pays the highest rate; a high-volume seller with a clean record pays the lowest.

Fast Shipping discount, if you're enrolled. Sellers who ship from pre-verified local inventory get a further discount off their seller-level rate, on top of whatever level they've already earned.

Payment processing fee. A flat percentage of the sale price, charged the same way regardless of seller level or Fast Shipping status.

Shipping to the verification center. What you pay to get the item to StockX. Unlike the two fees above, this is closer to a flat dollar cost — it does not shrink as a percentage just because the item is expensive.

Worked example: a $9 swing on the same $150 sale

Same item, same $150 sale price, same $100 cost to acquire it, same $6 to ship it in, same 3% payment processing fee. Only the seller fee and Fast Shipping status change:

FigureNew seller, no Fast ShippingHigh-level seller + Fast Shipping
Seller fee rate used9%4% base − 1pt Fast Shipping = 3%
Seller fee ($)$13.50$4.50
Payment processing (3%)$4.50
Shipping to verification$6.00
Total fees$24.00$15.00
Net payout$126.00$135.00
Net profit (after $100 cost)$26.00$35.00
Profit margin17.3%23.3%
Return on cost (ROI)26.0%35.0%

Same item, same sale price, same acquisition cost — a $9.00 difference in net profit, entirely from seller-level standing and a Fast Shipping enrollment. Multiply that gap across a month of sales and it is the difference between a target profit goal met or missed with nothing about the actual flipping changed.

Common questions

How much does StockX take from a sale?

Three deductions come out before payout: a seller fee that drops as your Seller Level rises (roughly 9% at the lowest level down toward 3% at the highest, minus a further Fast Shipping discount if you're enrolled), a flat payment processing fee on the sale price, and what you pay to ship the item to a verification center. On a $150 sale, a new Level 1 seller with no Fast Shipping keeps about $126.00 before their own cost of goods; a high-level seller with Fast Shipping enrolled on the same sale keeps about $135.00 — a $9.00 difference on an identical item at an identical price.

Does Fast Shipping actually pay for itself?

It reduces your seller fee by a fixed number of percentage points on every sale, so whether it pays for itself depends on your sale volume and the operational cost of keeping pre-verified local inventory ready to ship fast. On the worked example above, the discount alone is worth $4.50 on one $150 sale — multiply that by your typical monthly sale count to see whether it clears whatever Fast Shipping costs you to maintain.

Why does the same seller fee percentage cost more on some items than others?

It doesn't cost a different percentage — it costs a different dollar amount, because the fee is a percentage of the sale price. What actually shifts disproportionately is the flat shipping cost: it eats a much bigger share of a cheap item's payout than an expensive one's, so two sales at the same fee percentage can have very different effective take rates once shipping is folded in.

Is this StockX's official, current fee schedule?

No. Seller-level bands, the Fast Shipping discount, and the payment processing rate all change over time and can vary by seller, region, and category, and StockX does not publish a live feed a static page could read. Treat every rate here as an illustrative placeholder and confirm the actual numbers on your own seller dashboard and payout statements before relying on them.

Common questions

Why isn't the seller fee just one fixed percentage?

Because StockX's seller (transaction) fee percentage drops as your own Seller Level rises — more completed sales and a clean history earn a lower rate — and Fast Shipping enrollment knocks a further percentage off on top of that. Two sellers moving the identical item at the identical price can keep different amounts. This calculator treats both as numbers you supply from your own seller dashboard, not a fixed published rate.

Why does shipping cost matter more on a cheap item than an expensive one?

The seller fee and payment processing fee both scale with the sale price, but the cost to ship an item to a verification center is closer to a flat dollar amount regardless of what it sold for. That flat cost eats a much bigger share of a $40 sale than a $400 one, which is easy to miss if you only think in percentages.

Does this tool verify authenticity or track my inventory?

No. StockX runs its own authentication process, and this calculator never touches it. This tool only prices the payout and profit arithmetic of a sale you already made or are considering, from numbers you supply — it is not an inventory system, a sourcing tool, or a substitute for reading your own payout statement.

Does anything about my sales get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the sales list you type into the month section is never saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. The sale inputs above and the target monthly profit setting are different: those are saved locally on this device, so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-ebay-resale-fees.html.text:
← StockX seller payout calculator

StockX vs. eBay: the same sale, both fee structures

Every rate below is an illustrative example, not either marketplace's published fee schedule — both are inputs you should replace with your own seller dashboard numbers. What the worked example is useful for is the shape of the two fee structures: StockX tiers its seller fee by your own Seller Level and Fast Shipping enrollment and bills payment processing as a separate line, while eBay bundles processing into one final value fee and leaves outbound shipping to the buyer entirely up to the seller to arrange, rather than a flat verification-center drop. Not affiliated with eBay.

The item

A pair that sells for $200 on either platform. It cost $120 to acquire, plus $2 in packaging either way. On StockX, illustrative numbers: a 9% seller fee (no Fast Shipping), a 3% payment processing fee, and $6 to ship to a verification center. On eBay, illustrative numbers: a 13.25% final value fee plus a $0.30 per-order fee (payment processing already bundled in), and $12 to ship the pair directly to the buyer. Same pair, same price, same acquisition cost — only the platform and its fee structure change.

Fee by fee

Illustrative rates, not published schedules. Both are inputs you can change on the calculator.
On a $200 saleStockXeBay
Seller fee / final value fee$18.00 (9% seller fee)$26.80 (13.25% + $0.30)
Payment processing$6.00 (3%, separate line)$0.00 (bundled above)
Shipping$6.00 (to verification center)$12.00 (direct to buyer)
Other per-sale costs$2.00$2.00
Total fees$32.00$40.80
Net payout$168.00$159.20
Net profit$48.00$39.20
Margin24.0%19.6%

The structural difference matters more than the single-sale gap. StockX splits its cost into a seller fee that falls as your account's Seller Level rises, plus a flat processing percentage, plus a short hop to a verification center. eBay folds processing into one final value fee that does not depend on any seller-level ladder, but hands the seller the entire outbound shipping cost of getting the item to the buyer's door — which is usually farther, and pricier, than a verification-center drop. On this illustrative example, StockX nets about $9 more.

What would close the gap

Holding every rate fixed, eBay would need to sell this pair for about $210 — roughly $10, or about 5%, more than the $200 asked on StockX — to net a similar profit. Whether eBay's audience for a given pair actually clears a higher price than StockX's bid/ask market is a judgement about that specific listing, not something either fee schedule can answer.

What the fee comparison cannot tell you

Worth being direct about, because it is the honest half of this page. Fees are one input into which platform nets more on a given pair — they are not the only one:

  • Neither platform's current fee schedule is quoted here. StockX's seller-level bands and eBay's category-specific final value fee both change over time, and neither publishes a static rate an outside page can read live. Replace every rate above with the line on your own seller dashboard or payout statement before trusting the comparison.
  • Seller level, category, and shipping distance are yours, not a constant. A seller further along StockX's level ladder, or enrolled in Fast Shipping, pays less than the 9% used here. eBay's final value fee rate varies by category, and the $12 shipping figure above is a guess — a buyer across the country costs more to reach than one three states over.
  • Neither platform's authentication process, audience, or typical sell-through speed is compared here. StockX authenticates every sale itself before it reaches the buyer; eBay does not, outside whatever category-specific authenticity program it offers at the time. This page prices one hypothetical sale on each platform's fee structure — it says nothing about which one sells a given pair sooner, or what a buyer will pay for the same item on each.

Common questions

Is StockX or eBay cheaper for selling sneakers?

On the illustrative worked example here — a $200 pair, sold at a mid seller tier with no Fast Shipping, against an illustrative 13.25% eBay final value fee plus a $0.30 per-order fee and the seller paying to ship direct to the buyer — StockX nets about $9 more: $48.00 profit against $39.20. eBay bundles payment processing into its final value fee rather than charging it separately, but that is usually outweighed by the seller shipping straight to the buyer instead of to a nearby verification center, so the gap and even its direction depend on your own seller level, category fee rate, and shipping distance.

Why does eBay have no separate payment processing fee here?

Since eBay moved sellers onto its own managed payments, the final value fee already includes payment processing — there is no second processing line the way StockX and GOAT charge one on top of their seller fee or commission. That is a genuine structural difference, not a rounding choice: eBay's one fee does more of the work StockX splits across two.

Is this page affiliated with eBay?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by eBay Inc. eBay is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this comparison is about, using an illustrative fee structure rather than a claim about eBay's current published rates.

StockX vs. GOAT: the same sale, both fee structures

Every rate below is an illustrative example, not either marketplace's published fee schedule — both are inputs you should replace with your own seller dashboard numbers. What the worked example is useful for is the shape of the two fee structures: StockX tiers its seller fee by your own Seller Level and Fast Shipping enrollment, while GOAT tiers its commission by the item's sale price and bills a separate cash-out fee. Not affiliated with GOAT.

The item

A pair that sells for $200 on either platform. It cost $120 to acquire, plus $2 in packaging either way. On StockX, illustrative numbers: a 9% seller fee (no Fast Shipping), a 3% payment processing fee, and $6 to ship to a verification center. On GOAT, illustrative numbers: a 20% commission at this price band, a 2.9% + $0.30 cash-out fee, and a $5 shipping cost. Same pair, same price, same acquisition cost — only the platform and its fee structure change.

Fee by fee

Illustrative rates, not published schedules. Both are inputs you can change on the calculator.
On a $200 saleStockXGOAT
Seller fee / commission$18.00 (9% seller fee)$40.00 (20% commission)
Payment / cash-out fee$6.00 (3% processing)$6.10 (2.9% + $0.30)
Shipping$6.00$5.00
Other per-sale costs$2.00$2.00
Total fees$32.00$53.10
Net payout$168.00$146.90
Net profit$48.00$26.90
Margin24.0%13.5%

The structural difference matters more than the single-sale gap. StockX's seller fee is a percentage of the sale price that falls as your account's Seller Level rises, and Fast Shipping knocks a further discount off that same rate — so a high-volume seller pays a lower rate than the 9% used here. GOAT's commission is tiered by the sale price band rather than by seller history, and it bills a separate cash-out fee whenever funds are transferred out, on top of the commission. Two sellers moving the identical pair keep different amounts on either platform, for different reasons. On this illustrative example, StockX nets about $21 more.

What would close the gap

Holding every rate fixed, GOAT would need to sell this pair for about $227 — roughly $27, or about 14%, more than the $200 asked on StockX — to net a similar profit. Whether GOAT's audience for a given pair actually clears a higher price than StockX's bid/ask market is a judgement about that specific release, not something either fee schedule can answer.

What the fee comparison cannot tell you

Worth being direct about, because it is the honest half of this page. Fees are one input into which platform nets more on a given pair — they are not the only one:

  • Neither platform's current fee schedule is quoted here. StockX's seller-level bands and GOAT's commission tiers both change over time, and neither publishes a static rate an outside page can read live. Replace every rate above with the line on your own seller dashboard or payout statement before trusting the comparison.
  • Seller level and cash-out timing are yours, not a constant. A seller further along StockX's level ladder, or enrolled in Fast Shipping, pays less than the 9% used here. A seller who lets GOAT balance accrue rather than cashing out on every sale may avoid the cash-out fee entirely on some sales.
  • Neither platform's authentication process, audience, or typical sell-through speed is compared here. This page prices one hypothetical sale on each platform's fee structure — it says nothing about which one authenticates faster, which one's buyers pay more for a given release, or which one sells a given pair sooner.

Common questions

Is StockX or GOAT cheaper for selling sneakers?

On the illustrative worked example here — a $200 pair, sold at a mid seller tier with no Fast Shipping, and an illustrative 20% GOAT commission tier — StockX nets about $21 more: $48 profit against $26.90. StockX's seller fee drops as your Seller Level rises, while GOAT's commission is tiered by sale price band and is often higher at lower price points, so the gap and even its direction depend on your own seller level and the sale price. Neither rate here is a published schedule — replace both with the numbers on your own seller dashboard before trusting the comparison.

Why isn't there one fixed percentage for each marketplace?

Both platforms tier their seller-side fee rather than charging one flat percentage. StockX's seller fee falls as your account's Seller Level rises and falls further with Fast Shipping enrollment. GOAT's commission is tiered by the item's sale price band, and it also deducts a separate cash-out fee when funds are transferred out. A single quoted percentage for either platform is only ever true for one seller, at one price, on one day.

Is this page affiliated with GOAT?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by GOAT (Global Online Auction Technology / GOAT Group). GOAT is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this comparison is about, using an illustrative fee structure rather than a claim about GOAT's current published rates.

This calculator vs. tracking StockX payouts in a spreadsheet

Names no specific product or company — this compares a free calculator against the generic method most resellers already use: a personal spreadsheet with a payout formula typed in once and copied down for every sale.

QuestionSpreadsheet formulaThis calculator
Seller fee rate over timeA constant typed in once, easy to leave stale after a Seller Level change or a Fast Shipping enrollmentA field you update per sale, so a rate change never silently misprices an old row
Fast Shipping discount stacking on seller levelAn extra manual subtraction you have to remember to add and keep separate from the base rateApplied automatically and clamped so a discount can never push the fee below zero
Flat shipping cost vs. percentage feesOften typed in as another percentage, hiding that it hits a cheap item much harder than an expensive oneKept as its own dollar line, so the effective fee rate on a cheap item is visible rather than averaged away
Whole-month profit-goal checkA second sheet or a manual sum, often not kept in sync with the per-sale tabBuilt in — enter each sale's net profit and see the month total against your profit goal
History across sales and seasonsIts actual strength — a running log with item, size, and purchase datePrices one sale at a time; does not replace a flip log
Shareable single scenarioRequires sending the whole file or a screenshotOne link, via "Copy shareable link," with no file attached

Neither tool sets your seller fee, your payment processing rate, or what an item is worth — both are arithmetic on numbers you already have, and both are only as accurate as the figures you type in.

Common questions

Why not just track StockX payouts in a spreadsheet?

Plenty of resellers do, and a spreadsheet is a fine tool for tracking a flip list over a season. The failure mode is not the spreadsheet itself — it is that your seller fee rate is not a constant. It changes when your Seller Level changes and again if you enroll in or drop Fast Shipping, and a formula copied down a column keeps using whatever rate was true the day you typed it, silently understating or overstating profit on every sale after your level moves.

Does this calculator replace my flip-tracking spreadsheet?

Not necessarily. This tool prices one sale at a time and does not save a running list across sessions the way a spreadsheet's rows do. Many resellers use both: this calculator to get one sale's arithmetic right whenever their seller level or shipping enrollment changes, and their own spreadsheet to log the result alongside item, size, and purchase date for every flip over a season.
